title: Solar rebates in Australia, explained by state
description: Which solar and battery incentives are federal, which are state-specific, and what that means for the price you actually pay.
metaTitle: Solar Rebates in Australia by State (2026) | Advanced Solar Tech
metaDescription: A plain explanation of Australian solar and battery rebates: federal STCs, the federal battery rebate, and which states add their own schemes on top.
summary: Two incentives apply everywhere in Australia. A handful of states add a third. Confusing the two is the most common reason people misjudge what a system will cost them.

body.text: Australian solar incentives come in two layers, and most confusion comes from mixing them up. The federal layer applies wherever you live. The state layer does not.
The federal layer: applies everywhere

Small-scale technology certificates (STCs) are the main federal mechanism for solar. They are generated by your system based on its size, its location and the year it is installed, and in practice they are assigned to the installer and taken off your price up front. You do not claim them yourself. Two things about STCs are worth knowing: the certificate count steps down each year, and it varies by solar zone — the same system earns more certificates in Darwin than in Hobart.

The federal battery rebate is the second national scheme, reducing installed battery cost by roughly 30%. Like STCs, it is applied through your installer at the point of sale rather than claimed afterwards.
The state layer: applies in some places only

This is where the states diverge. Victoria offers Solar Victoria rebates and interest-free loans on solar panel systems, with eligibility set by property value, household income and whether a rebate has been claimed on that property before — but these do not extend to batteries. The ACT, WA and SA have run their own programs. NSW, Queensland, Tasmania and the NT rely largely on the federal schemes for system price.
If you are comparing quotes across state borders, check which layer each quote includes. A Victorian quote showing a state rebate is not comparable to a NSW quote that cannot include one.
What this means for your quote

A quote should show the system price, then each incentive as a separate line, then the amount you actually pay. If incentives are bundled into a single 'after rebates' figure, ask for the breakdown — it is the only way to check that everything you qualify for has been applied.
Program terms change, sometimes at short notice and sometimes mid-financial-year. Confirm current eligibility at the time you buy rather than relying on an article, including this one.

title: How to size a solar system properly
description: Why self-consumption matters more than system size, and how to work out the capacity that actually pays back.
metaTitle: How to Size a Solar System | Advanced Solar Tech
metaDescription: How solar system sizing actually works: reading your usage, why self-consumption beats export, and what roof and network limits do to the answer.
summary: The biggest system your roof fits is rarely the one with the best return. Here is what actually determines the right size.

body.text: Solar sizing gets presented as a single number — 6.6kW, 10kW, 13.2kW — but the number is an output, not an input. Four things determine it.
1. When you use power, not just how much

Energy you use as it is generated is worth your full retail rate. Energy you export earns a feed-in tariff, which is typically a fraction of that. Two households with identical annual consumption can get very different returns from the same system, purely because one is home during the day and the other is not.
This is why interval data matters. Your retailer can provide half-hourly consumption data, and it turns sizing from an estimate into an arithmetic problem.
2. What your roof can actually take

Usable area is not total area. Orientation, pitch, shading, obstructions, and the setbacks required around edges all reduce it. A north-facing array generates most over the day; east and west split generation toward morning and afternoon, which can suit some households better than a north-facing array producing its peak at noon when nobody is home.
3. What your network will let you export

Distribution networks cap export, and the cap varies by network and sometimes by street. In Victoria alone there are five distribution networks with different limits. A system sized past your export limit spends part of its life curtailed, generating power it is not allowed to send anywhere.
4. What you are likely to add later

A battery or an EV changes your consumption profile substantially. If either is likely within a few years, it is usually cheaper to specify the inverter, switchboard and cable runs for it now than to revisit the whole system later.
A well-sized 6.6kW system with high self-consumption can outperform a poorly matched 13.2kW system on return. Bigger is not automatically better.

title: Is a home battery worth it yet?
description: What actually determines battery payback, and the sizing mistake that undermines it most often.
metaTitle: Is a Home Battery Worth It? | Advanced Solar Tech
metaDescription: An honest look at home battery economics: what drives payback, why oversizing hurts, and when waiting is the better call.
summary: The federal rebate changed the arithmetic. It did not make every battery a good purchase — capacity that never cycles earns nothing.

body.text: Battery economics rest on one number: the gap between what your exported solar earns and what grid power costs you after sunset. Every kilowatt-hour the battery shifts across that gap is the return. Everything else is detail.
Why the arithmetic improved
Two things moved at once. Feed-in tariffs fell, widening the gap. And the federal battery rebate cut installed cost by roughly 30%. Both push in the same direction.
The sizing mistake

A battery earns money only on the energy it actually cycles. If your evening and overnight load is 8kWh and you install 20kWh, the top half of that battery rarely discharges — you have paid for capacity that sits idle. Payback is calculated on the whole purchase price, so unused capacity does not just fail to help, it actively extends the payback period.
Size from your actual post-sunset consumption. For most households that is a smaller number than expected.
When waiting is the better call

If your solar system is undersized, more panels almost always beat a battery on return per dollar. If you are about to move, the battery does not follow you easily. And if your evening load is genuinely small, the honest answer may be that storage does not stack up for you yet.
Backup during blackouts is a real benefit, but it is a resilience purchase rather than a financial one. Worth having — worth being clear that it is not what pays the battery back.
